records.source: Περὶ δὲ ὧν ἐγράψατε, καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι·
records.gloss: Concerning but [the things] which you wrote, good for a man a woman not to touch;
pieces: Now about the matters you wrote of. "It is good for a man to have no sexual contact with a woman."

L.1: Now concerning [the things] of which you wrote: "[It is] good for a man not to touch a woman."

R.1: Now I turn to the things you wrote to me about. Some of you say, "It is good for a man to keep away from sex with a woman."

decisions.choice: the words after the comma quote a saying from the Corinthians' letter, which Paul goes on to answer
alternatives: Paul's own statement, that it is good to stay away from sexual relations, which he then qualifies in verse 2
decisions.reason: Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, so where a quotation begins is an editorial judgment; the SBLGNT prints none here. Paul quotes the Corinthians' own sayings elsewhere in the letter and then corrects them ("All things are permitted for me", 6:12; "We all have knowledge", 8:1). Περὶ δὲ ("now concerning") turns to a question from their letter, as it does again in 7:25; 8:1; 12:1 and 16:1. Verses 2-5 then argue against married couples giving up sexual relations, which fits best if the saying came from some in Corinth who held that view. Yet Paul himself says that staying unmarried is good (verses 7-8, 26), so he may also agree with the saying in part.

decisions.choice: touch a woman: have sexual relations with her
decisions.reason: "Touch" was a common polite way of speaking of sexual relations, as in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 20:6 and Proverbs 6:29. The question is not about marriage as such, which comes up in verse 9, but about sexual relations, including within marriage (verses 3-5).

decisions.choice: a man ... a woman: a male and a female person
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπῳ (from ἄνθρωπος, a human being) stands here against γυναικὸς, so a man is meant. The saying is put generally, but verses 2-5 apply it to husbands and wives.

decisions.choice: Some of you say
decisions.reason: Readable says outright that the words are a saying from Corinth (m1), since quotation marks alone are easy to miss. Literal and Balanced show it with quotation marks.

decisions.choice: have no sexual contact with (B); keep away from sex with (R)
decisions.reason: In modern English "touch" would not be heard as sexual (m2). Literal keeps "touch".

records.heading: Marriage and sexual relations

records.source: διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω.
records.gloss: Because of but the sexual immoralities each [man] the wife of himself let him have, and each [woman] the own husband let her have.
pieces: But because sexual immorality is all around, each man is to have relations with his own wife. Each woman, too, is to have relations with her own husband.

L.2: But because of the sexual immoralities, let each [man] have his own wife, and let each [woman] have her own husband.

R.2: But there is a lot of sexual sin around you. So each man should have sex only with his own wife, and each woman only with her own husband.

decisions.choice: sexual immorality: sexual relations outside marriage, in all its forms
decisions.reason: πορνείας covers any sexual sin: chapter 5 deals with a man living with his father's wife, and 6:12-20 with men going to prostitutes. The plural points to actual cases, or to the many temptations, in a city like Corinth.

decisions.choice: have a wife, have a husband: have sexual relations with one's own spouse
alternatives: take a wife or a husband: get married
decisions.reason: "Have" a woman or a man can mean to have sexual relations with them (5:1, of the man who "has" his father's wife). Here Paul speaks to married people, as verses 3-5 show, and tells them to keep up sexual relations with each other, not to give them up. Some read it instead as advice to marry, which Paul gives to the unmarried in verse 9.

decisions.choice: each man ... each woman: the same command, in the same words, for both
decisions.reason: Paul speaks to the wife as directly as to the husband, with matching words, ἕκαστος and ἑκάστη, "his own" and "her own". The same balance runs through verses 3-4 and 10-16.

decisions.choice: have relations with (B); have sex only with (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "have" here (m2); Literal keeps the Greek wording. Readable's "only" says what "his own" and "her own" mean.

decisions.choice: sexual sin
decisions.reason: Readable uses plainer words for the same thing.

records.source: τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.
records.gloss: To the wife the husband the debt let him pay, likewise and also the wife to the husband.
pieces: A husband must give his wife what he owes her in marriage, and a wife must do the same for her husband.

L.3: Let the husband pay to the wife what is owed, and likewise also the wife to the husband.

R.3: A husband should give his wife what she needs from him in their sexual life, and a wife should do the same for her husband.

decisions.choice: what is owed: the sexual relationship each spouse owes the other
decisions.reason: ὀφειλὴν is a debt or obligation. Between verse 2 and verse 5 ("do not deprive one another") it is plainly a gentle way of speaking about sexual relations. Paul frames them as something given to the other, not taken.

decisions.choice: the obligation runs both ways, equally
decisions.reason: In the world of the time a wife's duty to her husband was taken for granted, and a husband's freedom much greater. Paul gives the husband the duty first and then says the wife has the very same one, ὁμοίως, "likewise".

decisions.choice: what he owes her in marriage (B); what she needs from him in their sexual life (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the idea of something owed and adds "in marriage"; Readable says plainly what is meant (m1).

records.source: ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.
records.gloss: The wife of the own body does not have authority but the husband; likewise and also the husband of the own body does not have authority but the wife.
pieces: The wife does not rule over her own body; her husband does. In the same way, the husband does not rule over his own body; his wife does.

L.4: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband [does]; and likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife [does].

R.4: A wife is not the one in charge of her own body; her husband is. And in the same way, a husband is not the one in charge of his own body; his wife is.

decisions.choice: have authority over: have the right to decide about, here in the sexual relationship
alternatives: own, in the sense of property
decisions.reason: ἐξουσιάζει means to have the right or power over something. Paul has used the related word in 6:12 ("I will not be mastered by anything"). In marriage neither partner decides alone about the sexual relationship; each has given the other a claim.

decisions.choice: the husband's body is under his wife's claim, as hers is under his
decisions.reason: That a husband had rights over his wife was a common view. That a wife had rights over her husband's body was not, and the second half of the verse matches the first word for word. Paul's point is the mutual claim, which leads into verse 5.

decisions.choice: rule over (B); be in charge of (R)
decisions.reason: Both put the idea of having the say over something in everyday words; Literal keeps "have authority over".

records.source: μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους, εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρὸν ἵνα σχολάσητε τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἦτε, ἵνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to the prayer and again on the same you may be, so that not may tempt you the Satan because of the lack of self-control of you.
pieces: Do not refuse each other, unless you both agree to it for a limited time so that you are free for prayer. Then be together again, or Satan may use your lack of self-control to tempt you.

L.5: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and [that] you may be together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

R.5: Do not say no to each other. The only exception is when you both agree to stop for a short time so that you can give that time to prayer. Then come back together. Otherwise Satan may tempt you, because you find it hard to control your desires.

decisions.choice: deprive: hold back from the other what is owed, here sexual relations
decisions.reason: ἀποστερεῖτε means to rob or defraud; Paul used it in 6:7-8 of believers cheating one another. Refusing sexual relations is withholding the "debt" of verse 3.

decisions.choice: the one exception has three limits: both agree, it is for a set time, and it is for prayer
decisions.reason: εἰ μήτι ἂν ("unless perhaps") makes the exception hesitant. ἐκ συμφώνου means by mutual agreement, not one partner deciding; πρὸς καιρὸν means for a season, not for good.

decisions.choice: be together again: resume sexual relations
decisions.reason: The phrase means to be in the same place, together. After the time of prayer the couple go back to their normal married life.

decisions.choice: lack of self-control: inability to master one's desires
decisions.reason: ἀκρασίαν is the opposite of self-control (compare verse 9). Paul expects married people to need their sexual relationship, and does not treat this as a fault to be ashamed of.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "devote yourselves to prayer ... be together again"
alternatives: "devote yourselves to fasting and prayer ... come together again"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "fasting and" before "prayer", and some read "come together" for "be together". The shorter text is found in the earliest manuscripts, and the mention of fasting is the kind of addition copyists made (compare Mark 9:29). Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: refuse each other (B); say no to each other (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what depriving means here (m1); Literal keeps "deprive".

decisions.choice: you find it hard to control your desires
decisions.reason: Readable turns the noun into a short clause and names what is hard to control.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ λέγω κατὰ συγγνώμην, οὐ κατ’ ἐπιταγήν.
records.gloss: This but I say according to concession, not according to command.
pieces: What I am saying here is a concession; it is not a command.

L.6: But this I say by way of concession, not by way of command.

R.6: I am allowing this, not ordering you to do it.

decisions.choice: this: the allowance in verse 5 for a time apart for prayer
alternatives: the instruction to marry or to keep up married relations (verse 2)
decisions.reason: τοῦτο most naturally points back to what Paul has just said. He allows a time of abstaining but does not require it; he would not call the married duty of verses 3-4 a mere concession. Some take "this" to cover verse 2 as well, so that marriage itself is allowed rather than commanded; verse 7 might support that.

decisions.choice: concession: something allowed, out of understanding, rather than required
decisions.reason: συγγνώμην means indulgence or allowance, a making room for people. It is set against ἐπιταγήν, an order or command. Paul is not saying he has no authority here; he is saying this point is permitted, not imposed.

decisions.choice: I am allowing this, not ordering you to do it
alternatives: by way of concession, not command
decisions.reason: Readable uses verbs in place of the abstract nouns.

records.source: θέλω δὲ πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἶναι ὡς καὶ ἐμαυτόν· ἀλλὰ ἕκαστος ἴδιον ἔχει χάρισμα ἐκ θεοῦ, ὁ μὲν οὕτως, ὁ δὲ οὕτως.
records.gloss: I wish but all men to be as even myself; but each own has gift from God, the one thus, the other thus.
pieces: I would like everyone to be as I am. Yet God gives each person a gift of {{gender:their|his}} own, to one this way and to another that.

L.7: But I wish {{gender:all people|all men}} to be as I myself also [am]; but each has {{gender:their|his}} own gift from God, one in this way, another in that way.

R.7: I wish everyone could be like me and not be married. But God gives different gifts to different people. One person has one gift, and another person has another.

decisions.choice: as I myself: unmarried, and able to live so without being troubled by desire
decisions.reason: Verse 8 shows that Paul was unmarried when he wrote. Whether he had been married before is not known. He had the right to take a believing wife with him on his travels (9:5) but chose not to.

decisions.choice: gift: a gift of God's grace, here the ability God gives for one's way of life
decisions.reason: χάρισμα is built from the word for grace (1:7). Paul calls his own way of life a gift from God, not an achievement, and says each person has one.

decisions.choice: one this way, another that way: both the unmarried life and married life are gifts from God
alternatives: the unmarried have one gift, and the married have other gifts of other kinds
decisions.reason: The two phrases are left open. In context the most natural reading is that some are given the unmarried life and others married life, so neither group should despise the other. Some read it more broadly, of the many different gifts of chapter 12.

decisions.choice: {{gender:all people|all men}} (L); {{gender:their|his}} (L, B)
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπους here means human beings, women and men; Balanced and Readable say "everyone", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: and not be married
decisions.reason: Readable says what "as I am" refers to (m1).

records.source: Λέγω δὲ τοῖς ἀγάμοις καὶ ταῖς χήραις, καλὸν αὐτοῖς ἐὰν μείνωσιν ὡς κἀγώ·
records.gloss: I say but to the unmarried and to the widows, good for them if they remain as also I;
pieces: Now I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is a good thing for them if they stay as I am.

L.8: But I say to the unmarried and to the widows: [it is] good for them if they remain as I also [am].

R.8: Here is what I say to people who are not married, and to widows: it is good for them to stay unmarried, just like me.

decisions.choice: the unmarried: unmarried people in general, or perhaps widowers in particular
decisions.reason: ἀγάμοις is masculine plural, which can include women. Because it is paired with "widows", some take it to mean men whose wives have died. In verses 11 and 34 the same word is used of a separated wife and of an unmarried woman, so it is not limited to men.

decisions.choice: good if they remain as I am: staying unmarried is a good choice, not a requirement
decisions.reason: καλὸν ("good") echoes verse 1, but here Paul speaks for himself and at once allows marriage (verse 9). μείνωσιν means to stay as one is.

decisions.choice: stay as I am (B); stay unmarried, just like me (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul's state was (verse 7, m1 there).

records.source: εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν, κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι.
records.gloss: If but not they exercise self-control, let them marry, better for it is to marry than to burn.
pieces: But if they are not keeping themselves under control, let them marry, for marrying is better than burning with desire.

L.9: But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn.

R.9: But if they are not controlling their sexual desires, they should get married. Being married is better than burning with desire.

decisions.choice: do not exercise self-control: they are in fact not managing to control their desires
decisions.reason: ἐγκρατεύονται is a plain present: Paul describes people who are actually struggling, not a mere possibility. It is the verb related to "lack of self-control" in verse 5.

decisions.choice: burn: burn with sexual desire
decisions.reason: πυροῦσθαι was used for being inflamed with passion as well as for literal burning (compare 2 Corinthians 11:29). The contrast with marrying points to desire; nothing in the passage speaks of judgment.

decisions.choice: burning with desire
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "with desire" so the figure is not taken as judgment (m2); Literal keeps "burn".

records.source: Τοῖς δὲ γεγαμηκόσιν παραγγέλλω, οὐκ ἐγὼ ἀλλὰ ὁ κύριος, γυναῖκα ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς μὴ χωρισθῆναι ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ, μενέτω ἄγαμος ἢ τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγήτω καὶ ἄνδρα γυναῖκα μὴ ἀφιέναι.
records.gloss: To the but having married I command, not I but the Lord, a wife from a husband not to be separated \v 11 if but also she be separated, let her remain unmarried or to the husband let her be reconciled and a husband a wife not to leave.
pieces: To those who are married I give a charge, and it is the Lord's, not mine: a wife is not to leave her husband.
If she does separate, she should either stay unmarried or be reconciled with him. And a husband is not to divorce his wife.

L.10: But to the married I command, not I but the Lord, [that a] wife is not to separate from [her] husband
L.11: (but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to [her] husband), and [that a] husband is not to leave [his] wife.

R.10: To married people I give a command. It does not come from me but from the Lord: a wife must not leave her husband.
R.11: But if she does leave him, she must not marry anyone else. Or else she should make peace with her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.

decisions.choice: not I but the Lord: Jesus' own teaching on divorce
decisions.reason: Jesus forbade divorce and remarriage (Mark 10:2-12; Matthew 5:31-32; 19:3-9; Luke 16:18). Paul passes on that teaching as a command of the Lord. In verse 12 and verse 25 he marks where he has no word of the Lord and speaks for himself.

decisions.choice: separate, leave: end the marriage; in practice, divorce
alternatives: a separation that leaves the marriage in place
decisions.reason: χωρισθῆναι and ἀφιέναι were both used for divorce in the Greek of the time. Under Roman law either spouse could end a marriage simply by leaving; no court was needed. That is why the wife who separates is called ἄγαμος, "unmarried". The two verbs vary the wording more than the meaning, though the wife is said to leave and the husband to send away.

decisions.choice: if she does separate ... : an aside within the Lord's command
alternatives: a separate instruction after the command
decisions.reason: The words in verse 11 interrupt the sentence, which then goes on with the husband's duty. Printed editions mark them off as a parenthesis. Paul allows for what may already have happened while keeping the command: such a wife is not free to marry someone else.

decisions.choice: leave (B, R wife); divorce (B, R husband)
decisions.reason: Both mean ending the marriage (m2); Balanced and Readable use the words a modern reader would use. Literal keeps "separate" and "leave".

decisions.choice: must not marry anyone else; make peace with her husband
decisions.reason: Readable says what staying unmarried means here and uses everyday words for reconciliation.

records.heading: The Lord's command on divorce

records.source: Τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς λέγω ἐγώ, οὐχ ὁ κύριος· εἴ τις ἀδελφὸς γυναῖκα ἔχει ἄπιστον, καὶ αὕτη συνευδοκεῖ οἰκεῖν μετ’ αὐτοῦ, μὴ ἀφιέτω αὐτήν·
records.gloss: To the but rest say I, not the Lord: if any brother a wife has unbelieving, and she consents to live with him, let him not leave her;
pieces: To everyone else I say this myself; it is not a word from the Lord. Suppose a brother has a wife who does not believe, and she is content to go on living with him: he must not divorce her.

L.12: But to the rest I say, I, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not leave her.

R.12: To the rest of you I say this. It is my own word, not a command from the Lord. If a man who is a believer has a wife who does not believe, and she is happy to stay married to him, he must not divorce her.

decisions.choice: the rest: believers married to unbelievers; I, not the Lord: Jesus left no saying on this case
alternatives: Paul's word carries less authority than the Lord's
decisions.reason: λοιποῖς are those not covered by verses 10-11: couples where only one partner has come to faith. Jesus spoke to married people within God's people; he gave no ruling on this new situation. Paul still speaks with an apostle's authority (verses 17 and 40; 14:37).

decisions.choice: brother: a fellow believer, here a man
decisions.reason: ἀδελφὸς is Paul's usual word for a member of the church. Here it means one particular kind of person, a believing husband; verse 15 names "the brother or the sister".

decisions.choice: unbelieving: not a believer in Christ
decisions.reason: ἄπιστον is used throughout this letter of people outside the church (6:6; 10:27; 14:22-24). It says nothing about the wife's loyalty to her husband.

decisions.choice: a man who is a believer
decisions.reason: Readable says who "brother" means here (m2).

decisions.choice: divorce
decisions.reason: As in verse 11, the verb means ending the marriage. Literal keeps "leave".

records.heading: Married to an unbeliever

records.source: καὶ γυνὴ εἴ τις ἔχει ἄνδρα ἄπιστον, καὶ οὗτος συνευδοκεῖ οἰκεῖν μετ’ αὐτῆς, μὴ ἀφιέτω τὸν ἄνδρα.
records.gloss: And a wife if any has a husband unbelieving, and he consents to live with her, let her not leave the husband.
pieces: And if a woman has a husband who does not believe, and he is content to go on living with her, she must not divorce him.

L.13: And if any wife has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not leave the husband.

R.13: And if a woman who is a believer has a husband who does not believe, and he is happy to stay married to her, she must not divorce him.

decisions.choice: let her not leave: a wife could end a marriage too
decisions.reason: Under Roman law a wife, as well as a husband, could divorce. Here Paul uses for the wife the same verb, ἀφιέτω, that he used for the husband in verse 12, and gives her the same rule.

decisions.choice: a wife: a believing wife, matching the "brother" of verse 12
decisions.reason: The parallel with verse 12 shows that she is a believer, as verse 14 confirms.

decisions.choice: divorce him
decisions.reason: As in verse 12; Literal keeps "leave" and repeats "the husband" as the Greek does.

records.source: ἡγίασται γὰρ ὁ ἀνὴρ ὁ ἄπιστος ἐν τῇ γυναικί, καὶ ἡγίασται ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄπιστος ἐν τῷ ἀδελφῷ· ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτά ἐστιν, νῦν δὲ ἅγιά ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Has been made holy for the husband the unbelieving in the wife, and has been made holy the wife the unbelieving in the brother; since then the children of you unclean are, but now holy they are.
pieces: For through his wife the husband who does not believe has been made holy, and through the brother she is married to, the wife who does not believe has been made holy. If it were not so, your children would be unclean; in fact, they are holy.

L.14: For the unbelieving husband has been made holy in the wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy in the brother; since otherwise your children are unclean, but now they are holy.

R.14: A husband who does not believe is made holy because of his wife, who believes. And a wife who does not believe is made holy because of her husband, who believes. If this were not true, your children would be unclean, not set apart for God. But they are holy.

decisions.choice: made holy: set apart and brought within the reach of God's holiness through the marriage, but not saved
alternatives: saved, or made a Christian, through the believing spouse
the marriage is acceptable to God
decisions.reason: ἡγίασται is the verb used in 1:2 and 6:11 of believers. But verse 16 shows that the unbelieving partner is not yet saved. Some in Corinth may have feared that union with an unbeliever made the believer unclean, as union with a prostitute did (6:15-17). Paul answers that the influence runs the other way: holiness reaches from the believer to the spouse and the home. How far this goes is not spelled out.

decisions.choice: in the wife, in the brother: by being joined to the believing spouse
decisions.reason: ἐν here gives the sphere or means: through the marriage bond with a believer.

decisions.choice: otherwise your children would be unclean: an argument from what the church already accepted
decisions.reason: ἐπεὶ ἄρα means "since otherwise". Paul assumes his readers already count the children of a believing parent as belonging to God; the same must then be true of the unbelieving spouse. "Unclean" and "holy" are the Old Testament terms for what may or may not come near God.

decisions.choice: through (B); because of (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek "in" means by virtue of the union (m2); Literal keeps "in".

decisions.choice: the brother she is married to (B); her husband, who believes (R); not set apart for God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced makes clear that "the brother" is the believing husband; Readable says so plainly and says what "unclean" means.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ὁ ἄπιστος χωρίζεται, χωριζέσθω· οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις, ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ἡμᾶς ὁ θεός.
records.gloss: If but the unbelieving separates, let him separate; not has been enslaved the brother or the sister in the such [cases], in but peace has called us the God.
pieces: But if the one who does not believe chooses to separate, let the separation happen. A brother or a sister is not bound in circumstances like these. It is in peace that God has called us.

L.15: But if the unbeliever separates, let [that one] separate; the brother or the sister has not been enslaved in such [cases]; but God has called us in peace.

R.15: But if the husband or wife who does not believe wants to leave, let it happen. In that case the believing husband or wife is not tied to the marriage. God called us so that we would live at peace.

decisions.choice: separates: chooses to end the marriage; let it happen
decisions.reason: χωρίζεται is the same verb as in verses 10-11, here of the unbelieving partner's own choice. χωριζέσθω tells the believer not to resist it.

decisions.choice: not bound: not obliged to hold the marriage together
alternatives: not enslaved to the unbeliever's wishes
decisions.reason: δεδούλωται means "has been enslaved", a strong word. The believer is not bound to keep a marriage the other has ended. Whether this also leaves the believer free to marry again is not stated; the text does not repeat the "stay unmarried" of verse 11, which some take as permission, while others hold that verse 39 still applies.

decisions.choice: God has called us in peace: a reason for letting the unbeliever go, rather than holding on at all costs
alternatives: a reason to keep the marriage if at all possible, leading into verse 16
decisions.reason: δὲ can mark a contrast or carry the thought on. Following "not bound", peace most naturally explains why the believer need not fight the separation. Others connect it with verse 16 as a call to keep the peace in the marriage.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "us"
decisions.reason: Some important manuscripts read "you" instead of "us". The two words differed by one letter and sounded alike, so copyists often confused them. The meaning is little changed. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: has not been enslaved (L); is not bound (B); is not tied to the marriage (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the strong verb; Balanced and Readable give its sense here (m2).

records.source: τί γὰρ οἶδας, γύναι, εἰ τὸν ἄνδρα σώσεις;
records.gloss: What for do you know, wife, whether the husband you will save?
pieces: How can you tell, wife, whether you will save your husband?

L.16: For how do you know, wife, if you will save the husband?

R.16: Wife, how do you know whether your husband will be saved through you?

decisions.choice: how do you know whether ...: you cannot be sure that staying will lead to your spouse's salvation
alternatives: perhaps you will save your spouse, so try to keep the marriage
decisions.reason: γὰρ links the question to verse 15. Read that way, Paul tells the believer not to hold on to an unwilling partner in the hope of winning them, since no one can know that. The question can also be heard hopefully, "who knows, you may save him", as a reason to stay (verses 12-13). The Greek allows both.

decisions.choice: save: bring the spouse to salvation, through faith in Christ
decisions.reason: σώσεις means to save in the full sense (1:18, 21). Paul speaks of the believer being the means of it (9:22); being made holy (verse 14) is not the same as being saved.

decisions.choice: your husband will be saved through you
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the wife is the means of his salvation, not its source.

records.source: ἢ τί οἶδας, ἄνερ, εἰ τὴν γυναῖκα σώσεις;
records.gloss: Or what do you know, husband, whether the wife you will save?
pieces: Or how can you tell, husband, whether you will save your wife?

L.16: Or how do you know, husband, if you will save the wife?

R.16: And husband, how do you know whether your wife will be saved through you?

decisions.choice: the same question, put to the husband
decisions.reason: Paul again speaks to husband and wife in matching words. The question carries the same meaning as the one before it (16a, m1).

decisions.choice: your wife will be saved through you
decisions.reason: As in 16a.

records.source: Εἰ μὴ ἑκάστῳ ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ κύριος, ἕκαστον ὡς κέκληκεν ὁ θεός, οὕτως περιπατείτω· καὶ οὕτως ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις πάσαις διατάσσομαι.
records.gloss: Except to each as has assigned the Lord, each as has called the God, so let him walk; and so in the churches all I direct.
pieces: Whatever the case, each of you should lead the life the Lord has given you, the life you had when God called you. I give this same direction in every church.

L.17: Only, as the Lord has assigned to each, as God has called each, so let each walk. And so I direct in all the churches.

R.17: But each of you should keep living the life the Lord has given you. Stay in the situation you were in when God called you. This is what I teach in all the churches.

decisions.choice: only, in any case: Paul turns from the exception back to the rule
decisions.reason: Εἰ μὴ, normally "except", here means "only" or "in any case". Having allowed that a marriage may end (verse 15), Paul states the general rule that governs the rest of the chapter: stay in the situation you were in when called. He says it three times (verses 17, 20 and 24).

decisions.choice: assigned, called: the place in life the Lord gave, and God's call to faith that came there
decisions.reason: ἐμέρισεν means to give each a portion or share. κέκληκεν is God's call that brought them to faith (1:9, 26). The two lines say the same thing from two sides: the situation the Lord gave, and the call that came to them in it.

decisions.choice: walk: live, conduct one's life
decisions.reason: περιπατείτω is Paul's usual word for a way of life (3:3; Colossians 1:10).

decisions.choice: I direct this in all the churches: the rule is not special to Corinth
decisions.reason: διατάσσομαι means to give orders or arrange. Paul often reminds the Corinthians that what he asks of them he asks of every church (4:17; 11:16; 14:33).

decisions.choice: lead the life (B); keep living the life (R)
decisions.reason: "Walk" in this sense is not everyday English; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: the life you had when God called you (B); the situation you were in when God called you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "as God has called" refers to (m2).

records.source: περιτετμημένος τις ἐκλήθη;
records.gloss: Having been circumcised anyone was called?
pieces: Was someone already circumcised when he was called?

L.18: Was anyone called having been circumcised?

R.18: Was a man already circumcised when God called him?

decisions.choice: circumcised: a Jewish man, marked by circumcision
decisions.reason: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 17:10-14). In a mixed church it marked out the Jewish men from the Gentiles.

decisions.choice: was called: was called by God to faith
decisions.reason: ἐκλήθη is passive with God as the one who calls (verse 17), as throughout this passage.

decisions.choice: when God called him
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who called.

records.source: μὴ ἐπισπάσθω· ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ κέκληταί τις;
records.gloss: Let him not draw over; in uncircumcision has been called anyone?
pieces: He must not try to reverse it. Was someone uncircumcised when he was called?

L.18: Let him not undo [his circumcision]. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision?

R.18: Then he should not try to undo it. Was a man not circumcised when God called him?

decisions.choice: undo: have the marks of circumcision hidden by surgery
decisions.reason: ἐπισπάσθω means "draw over". Some Jewish men in the Greek world had an operation to hide their circumcision, to avoid mockery in the gymnasium or to fit in (1 Maccabees 1:15). Paul tells Jewish believers not to do so.

decisions.choice: in uncircumcision: as a Gentile
decisions.reason: ἀκροβυστίᾳ, uncircumcision, stands for the state of a Gentile man.

decisions.choice: try to reverse it (B); try to undo it (R)
decisions.reason: The literal "draw over" means nothing to a modern reader (m1).

records.source: μὴ περιτεμνέσθω.
records.gloss: Let him not be circumcised.
pieces: He must not get circumcised.

R.18: Then he should not get circumcised.

decisions.choice: not be circumcised: a Gentile believer need not become a Jew
decisions.reason: Some taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised (Acts 15:1, 5; Galatians 5:2-6). Paul rejects this here as in his other letters.

records.source: ἡ περιτομὴ οὐδέν ἐστιν, καὶ ἡ ἀκροβυστία οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τήρησις ἐντολῶν θεοῦ.
records.gloss: The circumcision nothing is, and the uncircumcision nothing is, but keeping of commandments of God.
pieces: Being circumcised means nothing, and not being circumcised means nothing. What matters is obeying the commandments of God.

L.19: Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but [what matters is the] keeping of [the] commandments of God.

R.19: It does not matter whether a man is circumcised or not. What matters is doing what God commands.

decisions.choice: keeping God's commandments: doing God's will, which is what counts, not one's birth or mark
decisions.reason: The saying is startling, because circumcision was itself one of God's commandments (Genesis 17:10). Paul means God's will as now made known in Christ. Galatians 5:6 and 6:15 make the same contrast with "faith working through love" and "a new creation".

decisions.choice: but ...: the verb is left out
decisions.reason: After ἀλλὰ the Greek simply names "keeping of the commandments of God"; the meaning is that this, unlike circumcision, is what counts.

decisions.choice: what matters
decisions.reason: English needs a verb here (m2). Literal puts it in brackets.

records.source: ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ κλήσει ᾗ ἐκλήθη ἐν ταύτῃ μενέτω.
records.gloss: Each in the calling in which he was called, in this let him remain.
pieces: Each of you should go on in the place in life where God's call found you.

L.20: Each one, in the calling in which {{gender:they were|he was}} called, in it let {{gender:them|him}} remain.

R.20: Each of you should stay as you were when God called you.

decisions.choice: calling: God's call, together with the situation in which it came
alternatives: the call itself: remain as one called
decisions.reason: κλήσει is God's act of calling (1:26). Here, with "remain in", it takes in the circumstances of the person when the call came: married or single, Jew or Gentile, slave or free. It does not yet have the later sense of a job or career.

decisions.choice: remain: go on in it, without striving to change it for God's sake
decisions.reason: μενέτω is the key word of verses 17-24. It is not an absolute ban on change: Paul has allowed for separation (verse 15) and may encourage a slave to take freedom (verse 21). The point is that no situation needs to be changed to please God.

decisions.choice: the place in life where God's call found you (B); as you were when God called you (R)
decisions.reason: In modern English "calling" usually means a career or a sense of vocation; Balanced and Readable say what it means here (m1). Literal keeps "calling".

decisions.choice: {{gender:they were|he was}}; {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: Each one means every believer, women and men.

records.source: Δοῦλος ἐκλήθης;
records.gloss: A slave were you called?
pieces: Were you a slave when you were called?

R.21: Were you a slave when God called you?

decisions.choice: slave: a person legally owned by another
decisions.reason: Slaves made up a large part of the population of Roman Corinth, and many belonged to the church (1:26-28). A slave was the owner's property; many were freed later in life. Paul speaks to them directly, as members of the church.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free (verses 21-23): the Greek word means one who was owned (m1), and the passage turns on that.

records.heading: Called as a slave or as free

records.source: μή σοι μελέτω· ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ δύνασαι ἐλεύθερος γενέσθαι, μᾶλλον χρῆσαι.
records.gloss: Not to you let it be a care; but if even you are able free to become, rather make use.
pieces: Do not let that worry you. But if you do get the chance to become free, make the most of it.

L.21: Let it not concern you; but if indeed you are able to become free, rather make use [of it].

R.21: Do not worry about it. But if you have a chance to be set free, take it.

decisions.choice: rather make use of it: take the opportunity to become free
alternatives: rather make use of your present state: stay a slave even if you could be freed
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "rather use", with no object. Read with ἀλλ ("but") and εἰ καὶ as "if indeed", it makes an exception to the rule of remaining: take freedom if it is offered. The aorist χρῆσαι suits seizing a particular chance. Read with εἰ καὶ as "even if", it means "even if you can be freed, rather make use of your slavery", which fits the repeated "remain" of verses 20 and 24. Both readings have long been held, and the evidence is evenly balanced.

decisions.choice: do not let it concern you: being a slave does not lower a person's standing with God
decisions.reason: μελέτω means to be a worry or concern. Verse 22 gives the reason: in the Lord a slave is the Lord's freed person.

decisions.choice: become free: be set free by one's owner
decisions.reason: In the Roman world many slaves were freed, by their owner's choice or by buying their freedom with their savings. A slave could not usually decide it alone, so Paul speaks of being "able" to become free.

decisions.choice: make the most of it (B); take it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow the reading in m1 and say what is to be used: the chance of freedom. Literal keeps the Greek without an object.

records.source: ὁ γὰρ ἐν κυρίῳ κληθεὶς δοῦλος ἀπελεύθερος κυρίου ἐστίν· ὁμοίως ὁ ἐλεύθερος κληθεὶς δοῦλός ἐστιν Χριστοῦ.
records.gloss: The for in [the] Lord having been called slave a freedman of [the] Lord is; likewise the free having been called a slave is of Christ.
pieces: For a slave who has been called in the Lord is the Lord's freed slave; and in the same way, someone free who has been called is a slave of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.22: For the slave who was called in [the] Lord is [the] Lord's freedman; likewise the free [one] who was called is a slave of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.22: A slave whom God has called to belong to the Lord has been set free by the Lord. And a free person whom God has called has become a slave of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: freedman: a former slave set free by his owner, who still owed that owner loyalty
decisions.reason: A freed slave in Roman society took the former owner as patron and owed him honor and certain services. So the believing slave is truly free in the Lord, and at the same time belongs to him.

decisions.choice: called in the Lord: called by God into union with the Lord
alternatives: "in the Lord" describing the slave rather than the calling
decisions.reason: ἐν κυρίῳ goes most naturally with κληθεὶς: the call that brought the person to belong to the Lord.

decisions.choice: the free person is Christ's slave: both slave and free now stand on the same footing before Christ
decisions.reason: Paul turns both statuses around: the slave is free in the Lord, and the free person belongs to Christ as a slave belongs to a master. Paul calls himself a slave of Christ (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Verse 23 gives the ground: they were bought.

decisions.choice: freedman (L); freed slave (B); has been set free (R)
decisions.reason: "Freedman" is little used today; Balanced and Readable say what it means.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free and freed: the verse turns the two statuses around (m1, m3).

records.source: τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε· μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων.
records.gloss: Of a price you were bought; do not become slaves of men.
pieces: You were bought, and a price was paid for you. Do not become slaves of {{gender:human beings|men}}.

L.23: You were bought for a price; do not become slaves of {{gender:human beings|men}}.

R.23: God paid the price to make you {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own. So do not become slaves of {{gender:people|men}}.

decisions.choice: bought for a price: purchased, as in the slave market, by Christ's death, so that they now belong to God
decisions.reason: ἠγοράσθητε is the ordinary word for buying, and in this passage the picture is of a slave changing owners. Paul used the same two words in 6:20. The price is not named here; elsewhere it is Christ's death (Galatians 3:13).

decisions.choice: do not become slaves of human beings: do not let people be your masters in place of the Lord
alternatives: do not sell yourselves into slavery
decisions.reason: Some free people sold themselves into slavery to pay debts or to gain security, and Paul may have this in view. But the plural command is addressed to the whole church, slave and free, and most naturally means: do not let human opinions or demands rule you, since you belong to God.

decisions.choice: God paid the price to make you his own
alternatives: You were bought for a price
decisions.reason: Readable names the buyer and the purpose (m1).

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}} (L, B); {{gender:people|men}} (R)
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general.

decisions.choice: slaves
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it for people bought and owned, set against freedom: the verse turns on being bought (m1, m2).

records.source: ἕκαστος ἐν ᾧ ἐκλήθη, ἀδελφοί, ἐν τούτῳ μενέτω παρὰ θεῷ.
records.gloss: Each in what he was called, brothers, in this let him remain with God.
pieces: So, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, whatever your situation was when God called you, remain in it, living in God's presence.

L.24: Each one, in what {{gender:they were|he was}} called, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, in this let {{gender:them|him}} remain with God.

R.24: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, whatever you were when God called you, stay that way, and live close to God.

decisions.choice: with God: before God, living in his presence
decisions.reason: παρὰ θεῷ means "beside God" or "in God's presence". The situation stays the same, but it is now lived with God, which is what changes it.

decisions.choice: each in what he was called, in this let him remain: the rule of verses 17 and 20, given a third time to close the section
decisions.reason: The repetition rounds off the section on circumcision and slavery before Paul goes on to the unmarried in verse 25.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: As in 1:10, Paul writes to the whole church, women and men.

decisions.choice: living in God's presence (B); live close to God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "with God" means here (m1).

records.source: Περὶ δὲ τῶν παρθένων ἐπιταγὴν κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω, γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι ὡς ἠλεημένος ὑπὸ κυρίου πιστὸς εἶναι.
records.gloss: Concerning now the virgins a command of [the] Lord not I have, judgment but I give as having received mercy by [the] Lord trustworthy to be.
pieces: Now about those who have never married: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my opinion as someone the Lord in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercy has made trustworthy.

L.25: Now concerning the virgins, I do not have a command of [the] Lord, but I give [my] judgment as one who has received mercy from [the] Lord to be trustworthy.

R.25: Now about people who have never married. I do not have a command from the Lord about this. But I will tell you what I think. In {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercy the Lord has made me someone you can trust.

decisions.choice: virgins: people who have never married, chiefly young women of an age to marry
alternatives: anyone who is sexually inexperienced, whatever their state
decisions.reason: παρθένος named a girl or young woman who had not yet married, and so was presumed a virgin (Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:27). The form here could be masculine or feminine, and the word can be used of men (Revelation 14:4), but in this chapter it is always a woman (7:28, 7:34, 7:36-38). Paul has already spoken to widows and the married (7:8-16); now he turns to those who have never married. In 7:36-38 the word is used of one particular young woman, and its sense there is discussed on 7:36.

decisions.choice: a command of the Lord: a saying of Jesus that settles the question
decisions.reason: In 7:10 Paul could pass on a command of the Lord about divorce (Mark 10:9-12). On the never-married he knows no such saying, so he gives his own judgment (γνώμη), as in 7:12. He does not treat it as worthless: it comes from one the Lord has made trustworthy, and in 7:40 he claims to have the Spirit of God.

decisions.choice: having received mercy to be trustworthy: the Lord's mercy has made Paul reliable
alternatives: having received mercy because he was trustworthy
decisions.reason: The perfect participle ἠλεημένος describes a mercy received in the past whose effect lasts. The infinitive "to be trustworthy" gives the result of that mercy. Paul's reliability is God's gift (1 Timothy 1:12-13), not his own claim to merit. πιστὸς here means "reliable, worthy of trust", as in 4:2.

decisions.choice: those who have never married (B); people who have never married (R)
decisions.reason: "Virgins" puts the stress on sexual experience, while Paul's question is whether such people should marry (m1). Literal keeps "virgins". "Unmarried" is kept for ἄγαμος (7:32, 7:34), which can include the widowed and divorced.

decisions.choice: my opinion (B); what I think (R)
decisions.reason: Paul sets his considered view beside a command of the Lord. "Judgment" today can sound like a verdict on someone; Literal keeps it, and 7:40 uses the same words.

records.heading: Those who have never married

records.source: νομίζω οὖν τοῦτο καλὸν ὑπάρχειν διὰ τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην, ὅτι καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ οὕτως εἶναι.
records.gloss: I think therefore this good to be because of the present necessity, that [it is] good for a man the so to be.
pieces: So, because of the crisis we now face, I think this is good: it is good for a {{gender:person|man}} to stay as {{gender:they are|he is}}.

L.26: I think, then, that this is good because of the present distress: that [it is] good for a {{gender:person|man}} to be so.

R.26: Because of the hard times we are facing now, I think it is best for you to stay as you are.

decisions.choice: the present distress: a time of pressure and hardship already upon the believers
alternatives: a distress that is about to come
the ordinary constraints of married life
decisions.reason: ἐνεστῶσαν is a perfect participle of a verb meaning "to stand in, to be present" (Romans 8:38; Galatians 1:4, "the present evil age"). ἀνάγκην is constraint or distress (Luke 21:23, of the hardships before the end). Paul does not say what the distress is. It may be a local hardship in Corinth, or the pressures of the last days in general; 7:29-31 links it with the shortness of the time.

decisions.choice: this is good ... that it is good: the second clause spells out what "this" is
alternatives: "because it is good", giving a reason
decisions.reason: ὅτι can mean "that" or "because". Paul starts the sentence, breaks off, and restates his point: what is good is to stay as one is. The repeated καλὸν / καλὸν shows the restart.

decisions.choice: for a person to be so: to stay in one's present state, married or unmarried
alternatives: for a man to stay unmarried
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπῳ is general: anyone. "So" points to staying as one is, the rule of 7:17-24, and 7:27 applies it both ways: the married should not seek release, and the unmarried need not seek a wife.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}} (L, B); {{gender:they are|he is}} (B)
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπῳ means a human being of either sex. Readable says "you", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: the crisis we now face (B); the hard times we are facing now (R)
decisions.reason: "Distress" and "necessity" are no longer everyday words for a time of pressure. Literal keeps "present distress".

records.source: δέδεσαι γυναικί;
records.gloss: Have you been bound to a wife?
pieces: Are you bound to a wife?

L.27: Have you been bound to a wife?

decisions.choice: bound to a wife: married
decisions.reason: δέδεσαι is the verb Paul uses of the marriage bond in 7:39 and Romans 7:2. The question is addressed to a man ("you" is singular), but the principle applies to everyone (7:28).

decisions.choice: a question that sets up a condition: "Are you married? Then ..."
alternatives: a statement: "You are bound to a wife"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates it as a question. Either way the sense is conditional: if you are married, do not seek to be free.

decisions.choice: Are you married?
alternatives: Are you bound to a wife?
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture of being bound means (m1).

records.source: μὴ ζήτει λύσιν· λέλυσαι ἀπὸ γυναικός;
records.gloss: Not seek release; have you been released from a wife?
pieces: Do not try to get free. Are you free of a wife?

L.27: Do not seek release. Have you been released from a wife?

R.27: Then do not try to end your marriage. Are you single?

decisions.choice: release: ending the marriage by divorce
decisions.reason: λύσιν answers "bound": the release from a marriage is divorce, which Paul has already ruled out for believers in 7:10-13.

decisions.choice: released from a wife: not married now, whether never married, widowed or divorced
decisions.reason: The perfect λέλυσαι could suggest a bond once there and now loosed. But in pairing with "bound" it most likely just means "not tied to a wife", and 7:28 speaks of the unmarried in general.

decisions.choice: try to get free; free of a wife (B); try to end your marriage; single (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the pair "get free / free" for the Greek pair "release / released". Readable says what the release is (m1) and uses an everyday word for being unmarried (m2).

records.source: μὴ ζήτει γυναῖκα·
records.gloss: Not seek a wife;
pieces: Do not look for a wife.

R.27: Then do not go looking for a wife.

decisions.choice: do not seek: advice, not a ban
decisions.reason: The same words as "do not seek release" make the two cases match. 7:28 shows this is counsel: marrying is not a sin.

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ καὶ γαμήσῃς, οὐχ ἥμαρτες.
records.gloss: If but also you marry, not you sinned.
pieces: Yet if you do marry, you have done nothing sinful.

L.28: But if indeed you marry, you did not sin.

R.28: But if you get married, that is not a sin.

decisions.choice: if you marry, you have not sinned: marrying is no sin
decisions.reason: The aorist ἥμαρτες after a condition about the future looks at the act as complete: should you marry, the deed would not be a sin. Paul guards against anyone who took his advice as a rule (7:1, 7:36).

decisions.choice: you have done nothing sinful (B); that is not a sin (R)
decisions.reason: Says that the act itself is not sinful, which is the point of the aorist (m1).

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν γήμῃ ἡ παρθένος, οὐχ ἥμαρτεν.
records.gloss: And if marries the virgin, not she sinned.
pieces: And if a young woman who has never married takes a husband, she has done nothing sinful.

L.28: And if the virgin marries, she did not sin.

R.28: And if a young woman who has never married gets married, that is not a sin.

decisions.choice: the virgin: any young woman who has not yet married
decisions.reason: The article is generic: the class of such women, as in 7:25.

decisions.choice: a young woman who has never married
decisions.reason: As in 7:25 (r-en-1), the English names her state in life rather than her sexual experience.

records.source: θλῖψιν δὲ τῇ σαρκὶ ἕξουσιν οἱ τοιοῦτοι, ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῶν φείδομαι.
records.gloss: Affliction but in the flesh will have the such, I but you am sparing.
pieces: But such people will meet hardship in this earthly life, and I am trying to spare you.

L.28: But such [people] will have affliction in the flesh, and I am sparing you.

R.28: But married people will have troubles in their everyday lives, and I want to keep you from them.

decisions.choice: in the flesh: in ordinary bodily, earthly life
decisions.reason: σάρξ here is not the sinful human outlook of 3:1-3 but bodily life in this world (2 Corinthians 4:11; Galatians 2:20). Those who marry will face the pressures that come with a household, all the more in "the present distress" (7:26).

decisions.choice: affliction: pressure and hardship
decisions.reason: θλῖψις is a general word for pressure and trouble. Here it is the hardship of married life in hard times, not persecution as such.

decisions.choice: I am sparing you: I want to spare you, by this advice
alternatives: I will not say more, to spare you
decisions.reason: The present φείδομαι describes what Paul is trying to do in giving this counsel.

decisions.choice: hardship in this earthly life (B); troubles in their everyday lives (R)
decisions.reason: Follows the book-wide choices for θλῖψις (affliction, hardship, trouble). "In the flesh" is said plainly (m1), since in English it suggests sinful nature.

decisions.choice: married people
decisions.reason: Readable says who "such people" are: those who marry, the subject of the two sentences before.

records.source: τοῦτο δέ φημι, ἀδελφοί, ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος ἐστίν· τὸ λοιπὸν ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσιν, καὶ οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες, καὶ οἱ ἀγοράζοντες ὡς μὴ κατέχοντες, καὶ οἱ χρώμενοι τὸν κόσμον ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι· παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.
records.gloss: This now I say, brothers, the time shortened is; the remaining that both those having wives as not having be, \v 30 and those weeping as not weeping, and those rejoicing as not rejoicing, and those buying as not possessing, \v 31 and those using the world as not using fully; is passing away for the form of the world this.
pieces: Here is my point, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: the time has been cut short. So from now on, married men should be as though they had no wives,
those who weep as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, those who buy as though they kept nothing,
and those who deal with the world as though they did not use it to the full. For this world's present shape is passing away.

L.29: But this I say, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: the time has been shortened. From now on, [let] both those having wives be as not having,
L.30: and those weeping as not weeping, and those rejoicing as not rejoicing, and those buying as not possessing,
L.31: and those using the world as not using [it] to the full; for the form of this world is passing away.

R.29: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, this is what I mean. There is not much time left. From now on, married men should live as if they had no wives.
R.30: People who are sad should live as if they were not sad. People who are happy should live as if they were not happy. People who buy things should live as if those things were not really theirs.
R.31: People who use what this world offers should not get wrapped up in it. For this world, as it is now, is passing away.

decisions.choice: the time has been shortened: the time until the end has been drawn in, so that little remains
decisions.reason: συνεσταλμένος means drawn together or compressed. καιρός is the time God has set (Romans 13:11). Since Christ came, the present age is running out (10:11, "the ends of the ages"), and this shapes how believers hold everything in it. Paul does not name a date.

decisions.choice: from now on ... should: a call for how believers are to live
alternatives: "so that": the purpose for which God shortened the time
"the time that remains is short", joining these words to what comes before
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT places a raised dot before τὸ λοιπὸν, so these words begin the new clause. The clause with ἵνα can state God's purpose or give an instruction; either way it describes how believers are to live now.

decisions.choice: as not: living in each state without being ruled by it
alternatives: giving up marriage, grief, joy and possessions
decisions.reason: Paul does not tell husbands to leave their wives (7:10-13) or forbid weeping and rejoicing (Romans 12:15). Each "as not" means holding these things loosely, because none of them is lasting.

decisions.choice: the world: the present order of human life, with its goods, dealings and ways, which is passing
decisions.reason: κόσμος here is the world of everyday affairs that believers use and deal with: buying, owning and the like. It is not evil in itself, but it is not permanent. καταχρώμενοι means to use fully or use up; the believer uses the world without being consumed by it. σχῆμα is outward form or way of being (Philippians 2:8): the world as it now is passes away (1 John 2:17).

decisions.choice: cut short (B); there is not much time left (R)
decisions.reason: "Cut short" keeps the sense that the time has been shortened (m1); Readable says what that means for the hearers.

decisions.choice: this world's present shape (B); this world, as it is now (R)
decisions.reason: "Form" can suggest a document or a shape on paper; the point is the way the world now is (m4). Literal keeps "form".

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: The address includes the whole church, women as well as men, as the book-wide choice for ἀδελφός has it.

records.source: Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνους εἶναι.
records.gloss: I want but you free from care to be.
pieces: I want you to be free from cares that divide you.

L.32: But I want you to be free from cares.

R.32: I want you to be free from worry.

decisions.choice: free from care: not pulled two ways by competing concerns
decisions.reason: ἀμερίμνους begins a play on the verb in the next sentences: the unmarried "care for" the things of the Lord, the married also for the things of the world. Paul does not mean that the unmarried have no concerns, but that their concern is undivided (7:33-35).

decisions.choice: free from cares that divide you
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the word "care" that the next sentences repeat, and says what kind of care is meant (m1), so that the unmarried man's "care" for the Lord does not seem to contradict this wish.

records.heading: Undivided devotion to the Lord

records.source: ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῷ κυρίῳ·
records.gloss: The unmarried cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;
pieces: The unmarried man gives his care to the things of the Lord, how he may please {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.32: The unmarried [man] cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.

R.32: A man without a wife thinks about the things of the Lord and how to please {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: cares for the things of the Lord: gives his attention to the Lord's work and service
decisions.reason: μεριμνᾷ here is a good kind of care, as in 12:25 and Philippians 2:20. "The things of the Lord" are what concerns him: his service and his people.

decisions.choice: the unmarried man: any man without a wife
alternatives: a man who has never married
decisions.reason: ἄγαμος is broader than "virgin": in 7:8 and 7:11 it includes the widowed and the separated.

decisions.choice: gives his care to
decisions.reason: Keeps the word "care" from 7:32a and avoids "anxious", which would make his care for the Lord sound like a fault.

records.source: ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῇ γυναικί, καὶ μεμέρισται.
records.gloss: The but having married cares for the things of the world, how he may please the wife, \v 34 and he is divided.
pieces: But the married man gives his care to the things of the world, how he may please his wife,
and he is pulled two ways.

L.33: But the [one] who married cares for the things of the world, how he may please the wife,

R.33: But a married man has to think about the things of this world and how to please his wife.
R.34: So he is pulled in two directions.

decisions.choice: the things of the world: the everyday affairs of this life, such as a household and its needs
decisions.reason: κόσμος here is the world of 7:31: the order of ordinary life, which is passing. Pleasing one's wife is not sin; Paul has said husband and wife owe each other care (7:3-5). The point is that a married man's attention is shared.

decisions.choice: he is divided: his attention is split between the Lord and his wife
alternatives: "the wife and the virgin are also divided (different)", joining the verb to the next words
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the sentence after μεμέρισται, so the verb completes the description of the married man. Some manuscripts join it to what follows; see the note on the next sentence.

decisions.choice: pulled two ways (B); pulled in two directions (R)
decisions.reason: "Divided" alone can suggest a split mind or a broken loyalty; the picture is of attention drawn two ways (m2).

records.source: καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου, ἵνα ᾖ ἁγία καὶ τῷ σώματι καὶ τῷ πνεύματι· ἡ δὲ γαμήσασα μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσῃ τῷ ἀνδρί.
records.gloss: And the woman the unmarried and the virgin cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in the body and in the spirit; the but having married cares for the things of the world, how she may please the husband.
pieces: And the unmarried woman, or the young woman who has never married, gives her care to the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body as well as in spirit. But the married woman gives her care to the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

L.34: And the unmarried woman and the virgin care for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in the body and in the spirit; but the [woman] who married cares for the things of the world, how she may please the husband.

R.34: A woman who is not married, whether she was married before or has never married, thinks about the things of the Lord. She wants to be set apart for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in body and in spirit. But a married woman has to think about the things of this world and how to please her husband.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin care for ..."
alternatives: "There is a difference between the wife and the virgin. The unmarried woman cares for ..."
"the unmarried woman and the unmarried virgin"
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ here in several ways. The reading behind the King James Version joins μεμέρισται to the women ("the wife and the virgin are different") and has "the unmarried woman" begin the next clause. Other manuscripts place "unmarried" after "virgin" as well. The SBLGNT reading gives the clearest parallel to the unmarried and married man. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the unmarried woman and the virgin: a woman without a husband now (widowed or separated), and a young woman who has never married
alternatives: two names for the same woman
decisions.reason: ἄγαμος covers anyone without a spouse (7:8, 7:11), while παρθένος is the never-married woman of 7:25 and 7:28. Paul names both so that every woman without a husband is included. The singular verb treats them as one group.

decisions.choice: holy in body and spirit: wholly set apart for the Lord
decisions.reason: ἅγιος means set apart for God. "Body and spirit" means the whole person (2 Corinthians 7:1). Paul does not say married women are unholy; he has just called the believing household holy (7:14). The point is undivided devotion.

decisions.choice: whether she was married before or has never married; set apart for him
alternatives: the unmarried woman and the virgin; holy
decisions.reason: Readable says why Paul names two kinds of women (m2), and what "holy" means here (m3).

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν σύμφορον λέγω, οὐχ ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως.
records.gloss: This now for the of you yourselves benefit I say, not that a noose on you I may throw, but for the seemly and devoted to the Lord undistractedly.
pieces: I tell you this to help you, not to throw a noose over you. I want you to live as is fitting and to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away.

L.35: Now I say this for your own benefit, not that I may throw a noose on you, but for what is seemly and devoted to the Lord without distraction.

R.35: I am telling you this to help you, not to tie you down. I want you to live in a good and proper way and to give yourselves to the Lord without anything pulling you away.

decisions.choice: throw a noose on you: put a restraint on you, as one would catch an animal
decisions.reason: βρόχος is a noose or snare used in hunting or for restraining. Paul's advice is not meant to tie them down; marriage remains free (7:28, 7:36).

decisions.choice: what is fitting and devoted to the Lord: a life that is seemly and constantly at the Lord's service
decisions.reason: εὐσχήμων means proper or becoming. εὐπάρεδρον means sitting constantly beside someone, like an attendant waiting on a master. ἀπερισπάστως answers the "divided" man of 7:33-34: nothing drags such a person away.

decisions.choice: stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away (B); give yourselves to the Lord without anything pulling you away (R)
alternatives: devotion to the Lord without distraction
decisions.reason: Keeps the picture of sitting beside the Lord (m2), and says "without distraction" in plainer words.

decisions.choice: tie you down
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday idiom with the same sense (m1).

records.source: Εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν παρθένον αὐτοῦ νομίζει ἐὰν ᾖ ὑπέρακμος, καὶ οὕτως ὀφείλει γίνεσθαι, ὃ θέλει ποιείτω· οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει· γαμείτωσαν.
records.gloss: If but anyone to behave improperly toward the virgin of him thinks, if he be beyond-the-peak, and so it ought to be, what he wishes let him do; not he sins; let them marry.
pieces: Now if a man thinks he is not treating the woman he is engaged to rightly, because his desire for her is strong and the marriage ought to go ahead, he may do what he wants. He commits no sin. Let the two of them marry.

L.36: But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if he is past [the] peak, and so it ought to happen, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin; let them marry.

R.36: Suppose a man is engaged to a young woman, and he thinks he is not being fair to her. Maybe his desire for her is too strong, and he feels they should marry. Then he should do what he wants. It is not a sin for the two of them to marry.

decisions.choice: his virgin: the young woman a man is engaged to marry
alternatives: his unmarried daughter, whom a father may give in marriage
a woman living with him in a marriage without sexual relations
decisions.reason: The passage can be read in two main ways. (1) A man and the woman he is engaged to: he wonders whether he is treating her rightly by holding back from marriage, and Paul says they may marry; if he is settled in mind, keeping her as she is, unmarried, is also right. (2) A father, or guardian, and his unmarried daughter: he wonders whether he is wronging her by not giving her in marriage, and Paul says he may let the couple marry. The strongest point for (2) is that γαμίζω in 7:38 elsewhere means "give in marriage" (Mark 12:25; Luke 17:27). For (1): the man's own desire and will are stressed (7:37), "his virgin" is an odd way to name a daughter, and "let them marry" most naturally means the man and the woman. A third view, that the two lived together in a celibate marriage, has little support in the text. This translation takes (1), at every level.

decisions.choice: beyond the peak: his desire is strong, at full strength or more
alternatives: she is past the usual age for marriage
decisions.reason: ὑπέρακμος means "beyond the peak". The form can refer to a man or a woman, and the subject of ᾖ is not stated. Said of the man, it means that his passion is at its height or overflowing, which fits 7:9 and the contrast in 7:37, where the man has his desire under control. Said of the woman, it means she is past the bloom of youth, which would fit the father reading.

decisions.choice: behave improperly toward her: treat her in a way that is not right or honorable
decisions.reason: ἀσχημονέω means to act in an unseemly or shameful way (13:5). It may mean keeping her waiting without marriage, or the risk of sexual sin under strong desire (7:2, 7:9). Either way, marrying ends the problem.

decisions.choice: and so it ought to be ... let them marry: if marriage is the right course, the couple should marry
decisions.reason: "So it ought to be" refers to marriage as the fitting outcome. The plural γαμείτωσαν brings in both of them: the man and the woman marry each other.

decisions.choice: the woman he is engaged to (B); a young woman he is engaged to (R)
decisions.reason: Says plainly whom "his virgin" means on the reading taken (m1). Literal keeps "his virgin", which leaves the other reading open. "Betrothed" is no longer everyday English.

decisions.choice: his desire for her is strong (B); his desire for her is too strong (R)
alternatives: if he is past the peak
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "past the peak" means on the reading taken (m2).

records.source: ὃς δὲ ἕστηκεν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ ἑδραῖος μὴ ἔχων ἀνάγκην, ἐξουσίαν δὲ ἔχει περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, καὶ τοῦτο κέκρικεν ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ καρδίᾳ, τηρεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ παρθένον, καλῶς ποιήσει·
records.gloss: Who but stands in the heart of him firm, not having necessity, authority but has concerning the own will, and this has decided in the own heart, to keep the of himself virgin, well he will do;
pieces: But suppose a man stands firm in his heart. He is under no pressure, he has control over his own will, and he has decided in his own heart that the woman he is engaged to should stay as she is. He will do well.

L.37: But [he] who stands firm in his heart, not having necessity, but has authority over his own will, and has decided this in his own heart, to keep his own virgin, will do well.

R.37: But another man may have made up his mind firmly. He does not feel he must marry, and he is in control of what he wants. He has decided in his heart not to marry the young woman. That man will be doing what is right.

decisions.choice: under no necessity, with authority over his own will: not driven by desire, and free to decide
decisions.reason: ἀνάγκη is the same word as in 7:26, here an inner pressure: the strong desire of 7:36. Having ἐξουσία over his will means he is master of his desires (7:9). On the father reading, it would mean no outside pressure prevents him from deciding.

decisions.choice: to keep his virgin: to keep her as she is, that is, not to marry her
alternatives: to keep his daughter at home unmarried
decisions.reason: τηρεῖν means to keep or preserve. On the reading taken at 7:36 (m1 there), the man chooses not to marry. On the father reading, he keeps his daughter unmarried.

decisions.choice: that the woman he is engaged to should stay as she is
alternatives: to keep her as his betrothed
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the reading taken at 7:36 and says what keeping her means without going beyond the Greek. Readable says it plainly: "not to marry the young woman".

decisions.choice: He does not feel he must marry
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pressure is (m1).

records.source: ὥστε καὶ ὁ γαμίζων τὴν παρθένον ἑαυτοῦ καλῶς ποιεῖ, καὶ ὁ μὴ γαμίζων κρεῖσσον ποιήσει.
records.gloss: So that both the marrying the virgin of himself well does, and the not marrying better will do.
pieces: So the man who marries the woman he is engaged to does well, and the man who does not marry her will do better.

L.38: So then, both the [one] marrying his own virgin does well, and the [one] not marrying will do better.

R.38: So a man who marries the young woman he is engaged to is doing a good thing. And a man who does not marry will be doing something even better.

decisions.choice: marrying: taking her as his wife
alternatives: giving her in marriage, as a father gives his daughter
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in the New Testament γαμίζω means "give in marriage" (Mark 12:25; Luke 17:27), and that is the main support for the father reading of 7:36-38. On the reading taken at 7:36 (m1 there), Paul uses it here for the man who marries. The choice follows that decision.

decisions.choice: well ... better: both choices are good; not marrying is better in view of the present time
decisions.reason: Paul has given his reasons in 7:26-35: the present distress, the shortness of the time and undivided devotion to the Lord. He has also said marriage is no sin (7:28, 7:36) and that each person has his own gift (7:7).

records.source: Γυνὴ δέδεται ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς· ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνήρ, ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ·
records.gloss: A wife is bound for as much time as lives the husband of her; if but falls asleep the husband, free she is to whom she wishes to be married, only in [the] Lord;
pieces: A wife remains bound for as long as her husband is living. Should her husband die, she is free to marry whomever she wants, though only a man who belongs to the Lord.

L.39: A wife is bound for as long a time as her husband lives; but if the husband falls asleep, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in [the] Lord.

R.39: A wife is joined to her husband for as long as he is alive. But if he dies, she may marry anyone she wants, as long as he is a follower of the Lord.

decisions.choice: falls asleep: dies
decisions.reason: κοιμάομαι is a common way of speaking of the death of believers (11:30; 15:6, 15:18; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15).

decisions.choice: only in the Lord: she must marry a fellow believer
alternatives: she must marry in a Christian way, whoever the husband is
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" describes one who belongs to Christ (Romans 16:8-13). The limit most naturally applies to the man she marries. Paul allowed believers already married to unbelievers to stay married (7:12-14); this is about entering a new marriage (2 Corinthians 6:14).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "a wife is bound"
decisions.reason: Some later manuscripts add "by law", probably from Romans 7:2. The sense is not changed. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: dies
decisions.reason: The idiom (m1) is said plainly; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: only a man who belongs to the Lord (B); as long as he is a follower of the Lord (R)
decisions.reason: Says what "in the Lord" means here (m2).

records.heading: Widows

records.source: μακαριωτέρα δέ ἐστιν ἐὰν οὕτως μείνῃ, κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην, δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα θεοῦ ἔχειν.
records.gloss: More blessed but she is if so she remains, according to the my judgment; I think but I also [the] Spirit of God to have.
pieces: Even so, in my opinion she is more blessed if she remains a widow. And I believe that I too have the Spirit of God.

L.40: But she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment; and I think that I also have [the] Spirit of God.

R.40: But I think she will be better off if she does not marry again. And I believe God's Spirit is guiding me too.

decisions.choice: more blessed: better off, in the fuller sense of a life given to the Lord without distraction
decisions.reason: μακάριος is the word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11). Paul's reasons for preferring that she stay unmarried are those of 7:26-35, not merely her contentment.

decisions.choice: I think that I too have the Spirit of God: a modest but firm claim to the Spirit's guidance
alternatives: real uncertainty about whether he has the Spirit
decisions.reason: δοκῶ is restrained, perhaps with irony, and κἀγὼ ("I too") suggests that some in Corinth claimed the Spirit for their own views (14:37). Paul's opinion is not a command of the Lord (7:25), but it is given by one led by God's Spirit (2:12-16).

decisions.choice: if she remains a widow (B); if she does not marry again (R)
decisions.reason: Says what "so" refers to: the widow of 7:39 staying unmarried.

decisions.choice: God's Spirit is guiding me too
alternatives: I too have the Spirit of God
decisions.reason: Readable says what having the Spirit means for Paul's advice (m2).
